title: Method selection
audience: Carpet and upholstery cleaners who choose a method for a job after inspection and testing.
referencesAtStart: Official sources: Safe Work Australia, Hazardous chemicals register (no date shown); Safe Work Australia, Understanding safety data sheets for hazardous chemicals (fact sheet) (no date shown in the text read; file path 2021-11); WorkSafe Victoria, The hierarchy of control (reviewed 30/07/2022); WorkSafe ACT, Electrical equipment (no date shown); Safe Work Australia, Model Code of Practice: Hazardous manual tasks (no date or edition shown).
learningOutcomes: Compare dry, low-moisture and wet methods and choose the one that suits the fibre and the soil.
Explain the risks of each method, including shrinkage, colour change, residue and wicking.
Refuse a method that is not suitable for the fibre or the construction.

instruction.heading: The main methods
instruction.body: Cleaning methods for carpet and upholstery are usually grouped by how much water they put into the item. Dry methods use powders or compounds that are worked into the pile and then removed by vacuuming, and they add little or no water. Low-moisture methods use a small amount of water or solution, worked in with pads or rotary equipment, and they leave the item damp rather than wet. Wet methods, including hot-water extraction, inject a larger volume of solution and then pull it back out. Equipment makers and suppliers use their own names for these approaches, so the name of a method matters less than the water load, the dwell time, the residue left behind and the drying time. The general practice is that the method is chosen from the fibre, the construction, the soil and the test result, not from habit.

instruction.heading: Choosing the method
instruction.body: Work through five questions before any method is chosen. What is the fibre group, and is it treated as sensitive? What is the construction, and in particular is the backing woven, latex-backed or otherwise slow to dry? What is the soil: dry grit, greasy soil, a protein stain or a dye stain? What did the test show on an inconspicuous area? How long can the item stay out of use, and what drying time is practical in the room or the premises? The answers point to a method. Where two methods are both possible, choose the one that puts less water into the item, and move up to the wetter method only if the lighter method has been tried and has not worked. Record the reasons for the choice.

instruction.heading: Risks of each method
instruction.body: Wet methods carry the most risk of shrinkage, colour bleed, wicking of soil and product to the backing, and a long drying time. They can also leave a residue that attracts soil if the rinse is poor, and a backing can delaminate if it is over-wetted. Low-moisture methods can leave residue behind if the product is not fully removed, and they can build up soil if the pads are not changed often enough. Dry methods can grind soil deeper into the pile if they are used without enough vacuuming, and they remove less soil from heavily soiled areas. Explain the risks to the customer in plain terms, and record the explanation and the customer's agreement.

instruction.heading: Equipment, settings and electrical checks
instruction.body: Set the machine as the equipment maker's manual directs, including the water temperature, the solution flow, the pressure and the tank levels. Do not set the water hotter than the method and the test allow, and do not exceed the setting the maker gives. Before each use, look over the hoses, the tank, the cord and the plug for damage. WorkSafe ACT's guidance on electrical equipment describes an external inspection of the cords and connections as one of the checks, with protective earth, insulation and polarity testing to AS/NZS 3760:2022, and says that a licensed electrician or a person certified as competent carries out the testing (fetched 2026-11-03). Keep a record of the last test date and the tag on each machine.

instruction.heading: Drying, residue and the job's pace
instruction.body: Plan the drying before the method starts. Confirm how long the item needs to dry in the conditions on site, and keep traffic off until it is dry. A method that leaves the item wet for many hours is a poor choice for a room that must be used that evening. Remove product residue as the label directs. Where the label does not give a rinse step, the general practice is to extract the residue with clean water as the method allows, and to check for tide marks after drying. Record the drying time and the residue check.

instruction.heading: Refusing an unsuitable method and offering an alternative
instruction.body: Refuse a method that is not suitable, such as hot water on a wool carpet, or extraction on a woven backing that cannot be dried in the time available. Do not accept the booking simply because the customer asked for the method. Offer a conservative alternative, such as a low-moisture method after a test, or a dry method for a sensitive item, and explain what that alternative can and cannot do. Record the refusal, the reason, the alternative offered and the customer's response. A refusal written down at the time protects both the business and the customer.

instruction.heading: Wastewater and the work site
instruction.body: Wet methods produce wastewater that contains soil and product. The research brief for this course treats discharge to stormwater as out of bounds. Record how the water was disposed of.

procedure: Choose the method from the fibre, the construction, the soil and the test result, and record the reasons.
Check the machine: the water temperature, the solution flow, the hoses, the cord, and the test date and tag.
Plan the drying time for the conditions on site, and confirm that traffic can be kept off.
Explain the risks to the customer: shrinkage, colour bleed, residue, wicking and drying time.
Refuse any method that is unsuitable for the fibre or the construction, and offer a conservative alternative.
Record the method, the reasons, the risks explained, the customer's agreement, and any refusal and alternative offered.
Record the drying time, the residue check and how the wastewater was disposed of.

workedExamples.situation: A customer wants hot-water extraction on a woven wool rug. The owner says the rug will be needed again the same evening.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What method do you recommend, and what do you say about the drying time?
workedExamples.reasoning: Refuse hot-water extraction. The wool may shrink, and the woven backing may hold water for longer than the evening allows. Explain the risks in plain terms. Recommend a conservative low-moisture method after a test on an inconspicuous edge, and say honestly that it may not remove every mark. If the rug must be used the same evening, offer a method that leaves it dry sooner, or propose that the rug is cleaned on another day. Record the refusal, the reasons, the alternative and the customer's response.

workedExamples.situation: (Example job) A loop-pile synthetic office carpet has a greasy soil line at the entry. The test on an inconspicuous spot shows no colour change or residue with a low-moisture method, but the soil does not fully lift.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Do you move to hot-water extraction?
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not move to a wetter method without a reason. Check the test result again, and confirm that the drying time is acceptable for the room. If a wetter method is then considered, repeat the test with that method on an inconspicuous area first, explain the extra water and drying time to the client, and record the decision. Record that the soil may not fully lift and that the limit was agreed.

workedExamples.situation: (Example job) A cotton upholstered sofa with a loose cover shows a coloured hem. The owner wants a wet method across the whole sofa.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which method do you use, and what is the test?
workedExamples.reasoning: Test the planned method on an inconspicuous area, such as the underside of the cushion, and check a white cloth for transfer. If the dye moves, do not use a wet method on that cover. Offer a dry or low-moisture approach that suits the test result, explain its limits, and record the test, the result and the decision. Check whether the cover can be removed and cleaned as the maker directs, and record that as a separate option.

equipmentAndPpe: Approved carpet and upholstery products, each with its label and current safety data sheet
Extraction, low-moisture and drying equipment, checked before use, with a test date and tag on each machine
Hoses, cords and plugs inspected for damage before each use
Gloves and eye protection, as set by the product's safety data sheet
Respiratory protection only where the safety data sheet directs it, after ventilation and the wetter method have been considered
White test cloth, timer and job record for the method decision

commonErrors.prevention: Choose from the fibre, construction, soil and test result, and record the reasons.

commonErrors.error: Leaving product residue that attracts soil.
commonErrors.prevention: Remove the residue as the label directs, and check for tide marks after drying.

commonErrors.error: Extracting a woven backing that cannot dry in the time available.
commonErrors.prevention: Choose a low-moisture method and confirm the drying time before starting.

commonErrors.error: Using a machine with a damaged cord or an overdue test tag.
commonErrors.prevention: Inspect the machine before use and do not use it until it is tested and tagged.

commonErrors.error: Accepting a method the customer asked for without checking its suitability.
commonErrors.prevention: Refuse an unsuitable method, offer an alternative, and record the refusal.
Check the local rule and any trade-waste requirement before the job, and record the disposal.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Hazardous chemicals on the workplace register must each be matched to a current safety data sheet, and the register must be kept where workers can reach it (Safe Work Australia, hazardous chemicals register, fetched 2026-11-03; no date shown).

A supplier provides the sheet at no cost on first supply or on request. The sheet has 16 headings, and it should have been prepared within the last five years (Safe Work Australia, Understanding safety data sheets, fetched 2026-11-03).

Personal protective equipment sits at the bottom of the hierarchy of control, where it is judged the weakest option. Elimination and substitution come before it (WorkSafe Victoria, The hierarchy of control, reviewed 30/07/2022).

In the ACT, the WorkSafe guidance on electrical equipment used at work refers to inspection and testing to AS/NZS 3760:2022, and says the testing is done by a licensed electrician or a person certified as competent (WorkSafe ACT, Electrical equipment, fetched 2026-11-03).
Moving extraction machines, furniture and rugs are manual tasks. Safe Work Australia's model Code of Practice says that the risks must be identified, assessed and controlled (fetched 2026-11-03).
Product-specific dilution, dwell time and PPE come from the product label and SDS.

knowledgeChecks.question: A woven wool rug is booked for hot-water extraction. What is correct?
options: Do it as booked, since the client has already agreed to the method
Refuse it, and offer a conservative low-moisture method after a test
Use the hottest water the machine can produce to lift the stain fast

knowledgeChecks.question: What is a risk of wet methods?
options: Faster drying of the carpet fibres in general
Less soil removed in every case, so the work is quicker
Shrinkage, colour bleed and wicking to the backing

knowledgeChecks.question: How is the method chosen?
options: From the fibre, construction, soil and test result
By habit, since the crew always does it the same way
By the cheapest product on the truck that day
